strengths: The reconstruction results demonstrate a worthwhile improvement on challenging viewpoints. In Table 2, extreme-view LPIPS improves over the strongest baseline from 0.3492 to 0.2866 on Ava-256 and from 0.3098 to 0.2154 on NeRSemble, alongside substantial improvements in identity distance and PSNR.

Evaluation includes both held-out NeRSemble identities and an unseen dataset, Ava-256. Figures 3, 8, and 9 visually support improved robustness to side and elevated views. The supplement specifies evaluation identities and describes consistent cropping across methods.

Combining DINOv2 and SAM2.1 features provides a useful perceptual supervision strategy. Table 3 supports complementary benefits, particularly for identity preservation, and includes comparisons without the CNN refinement stage.

The segmentation- and CLIP-conditioned editing extension demonstrates potentially useful image-guided and zero-shot text-guided control. The shared reconstruction and editing framework is clearly explained, and training on a single RTX 3090 suggests accessible computational requirements.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is materially limited. The manuscript and supplement omit training-set sizes and mixture ratios, optimizer settings, batch size, image resolution, loss weights and feature aggregation details, and substantial encoder/decoder configuration information. Exact evaluation view pairs, camera handling, and baseline inference settings are also insufficiently specified.

The claimed architectural contribution is not isolated experimentally. There are no ablations of the dual-branch encoder, omission of 3D self-attention, or patch construction, and no controlled comparison separating architectural gains from the different training data and losses. Several major components are explicitly inherited from LAM, MAE, and GRM.

The loss evidence supports a tradeoff rather than broad superiority over conventional supervision. Without CNN refinement, the proposed loss improves ArcFace but has worse PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS than LPIPS+L1; DreamSim changes only from 0.1179 to 0.1161. With refinement, LPIPS changes from 0.2877 to 0.2866. Using a shared CNN trained on an earlier model complicates attribution, and no variability estimates establish the reliability of these small differences.

Strong geometry/style disentanglement is not established by the qualitative editing examples. A global CLIP embedding can encode shape-related attributes, while segmentation maps contain appearance-correlated semantic information; their input formats do not guarantee independence. There are no quantitative geometry-preservation tests, systematic conditioning swaps, or comparisons against existing editing methods.

The evaluation supports novel-view image quality more directly than accurate 3D geometry or arbitrary-view consistency. All quantitative metrics assess rendered images after a 2D refinement network, with no direct geometry or cross-view consistency measurements. Evaluation covers only 16 identities, and the temporal-consistency claim rests on two qualitative video examples.

Overall, the substantial extreme-view reconstruction gains place this near the acceptance boundary, but incomplete reproducibility and insufficient isolation of the architectural, perceptual-loss, and disentanglement claims prevent a stronger recommendation. These concerns extend beyond presentation refinements.

strengths: The reconstruction results are meaningful, especially for extreme viewpoints. In Table 2, PercHead improves Ava-256 LPIPS from the strongest baseline's 0.3492 to 0.2866 and ArcFace distance from 0.4163 to 0.2812. Gains also hold on NeRSemble and across multiple metrics, rather than only the proposed perceptual objective.

Evaluation includes an unseen dataset, Ava-256, alongside held-out NeRSemble identities. Figures 3, 8, and 9 support the quantitative findings with visibly better preservation of facial structure under substantial viewpoint changes. The supplement documents evaluation identities and cropping alignment.

Combining DINOv2 and SAM features for supervision is a plausible, useful empirical contribution. Table 3 includes individual-loss, training-data, and CNN ablations, and demonstrates an identity-preservation benefit over conventional LPIPS+L1 supervision.

The segmentation-and-style editing interface offers a useful extension of the reconstruction model. The examples demonstrate promising image-conditioned appearance transfer and zero-shot text conditioning without text-specific training.
weaknesses: The principal concern is insufficient isolation of the claimed methodological contribution. There are no ablations of the dual-branch encoder, removal of decoder self-attention, or template-based patch design. These components largely adapt established mechanisms, and comparisons against systems trained with different data do not establish which proposed changes explain the substantial reconstruction gains.

The evidence for broadly superior perceptual supervision is mixed. In Table 3, the full model improves ArcFace over LPIPS+L1, but LPIPS changes only from 0.2877 to 0.2866 while PSNR and SSIM worsen. Without the CNN, the proposed loss has worse LPIPS (0.3010 versus 0.2897) and only a small DreamSim improvement (0.1161 versus 0.1179). All variants use a CNN trained on an earlier model, leaving compatibility with that fixed postprocessor as a possible influence. The results support a tradeoff favoring identity preservation more clearly than general superiority.

Reproducibility is materially limited. The manuscript and supplement omit important settings such as training-set sizes and mixture ratios, view-pair sampling, image resolution, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, loss weights and feature aggregation, and detailed encoder/decoder configurations. Evaluation identities are supplied, but exact camera-pair selection and baseline configuration details remain insufficient to reconstruct the reported benchmark reliably.

The claim of independent geometry and style control is stronger than the evidence. A global CLIP embedding can retain shape-related information, and a single segmentation map does not uniquely specify 3D geometry; the input modalities therefore do not themselves ensure disentanglement. Figures 5 and 6 provide examples, but there are no quantitative geometry-preservation or edit-adherence measurements and no comparisons with editing methods discussed in related work.

The evaluation supports improved rendered novel views more directly than accurate 3D geometry or consistency across arbitrary viewpoints. Metrics operate on images after a view-specific CNN, with no direct geometry assessment or explicit cross-view consistency measurement. The 11 Ava-256 and five NeRSemble identities also lack per-subject variability estimates, making small ablation differences difficult to interpret.

Overall, the reconstruction gains make this a worthwhile submission, but the unresolved attribution of those gains, incomplete specification, and unsupported strength of the disentanglement claim currently favor weak rejection. These are substantive evidentiary concerns rather than merely presentation issues or a demand for broader benchmark coverage.

strengths: The strongest contribution is improved reconstruction under large viewpoint changes. In Table 2, extreme-view LPIPS improves over the best compared baseline from 0.3492 to 0.2866 on Ava-256 and from 0.3098 to 0.2154 on NeRSemble, with substantial improvements in identity distance. Figures 3, 8, and 9 visually support these gains.

Evaluation includes both held-out NeRSemble identities and an entirely unseen dataset, Ava-256, with four relevant baselines and complementary image-quality and identity metrics. The supplement specifies evaluation identities and efforts to standardize crops and backgrounds.

Combining DINOv2 and SAM2.1 supervision is a useful empirical contribution. Table 3 shows complementary benefits over either loss alone, particularly for identity preservation, and demonstrates that useful 3D reconstruction can be learned without conventional reconstruction losses in the lifting stage.

The shared reconstruction and editing pipeline is coherent and potentially useful. Figures 5 and 6 demonstrate promising segmentation-conditioned generation and text-driven appearance changes without text-specific training.

Overall, the supported extreme-view reconstruction improvements and useful perceptual-supervision finding favor acceptance, despite meaningful limitations in attribution, reproducibility, and editing validation.
weaknesses: The evidence for broadly superior perceptual supervision is mixed. Without the CNN, the proposed loss underperforms LPIPS+L1 on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS; its DreamSim improvement is small, although identity distance improves. With the CNN, LPIPS improves only from 0.2877 to 0.2866. Moreover, all ablations share a CNN trained on an earlier model, which may interact differently with each variant. Table 3 supports a tradeoff more clearly than overall superiority.

The architecture's individual contributions are not isolated. There are no ablations of the task-specific encoder branch, omission of 3D self-attention, or patch initialization. Because the system also combines several training datasets, the baseline comparisons do not establish how much improvement comes from architecture, supervision, or data.

Reproducibility is materially limited by missing training and implementation details, including dataset sizes and sampling ratios, optimizer settings, input resolution, transformer dimensions, loss weights and feature aggregation, and CNN architecture. Reporting GPU hours and evaluation identities is helpful but insufficient to reproduce the method.

The quantitative evaluation covers only 16 identities, without uncertainty estimates or per-subject results. Exact view-pair selection and angular ranges are insufficiently specified. Rendered-image metrics support novel-view quality but do not directly establish accurate geometry or consistency across arbitrary viewpoints, especially after view-wise CNN refinement.

Geometry/style disentanglement is asserted more strongly than demonstrated. A global CLIP embedding can encode shape-related information, and segmentation maps retain appearance-related attributes such as hairstyle. Selected qualitative examples, without geometry-preservation measurements, editing comparisons, or systematic style swaps, establish promising controllability rather than reliable disentanglement.

Practical editing remains slow: the supplement reports 10 seconds for text stylization and 28 seconds for reference-image stylization. The acknowledged lack of real-time inference and expression transfer limits several proposed avatar applications.

strengths: The strongest contribution is robust single-image reconstruction under large viewpoint changes. On Ava-256 extreme views, PercHead improves PSNR from the best baseline's 14.3 to 15.9, LPIPS from 0.349 to 0.291, and ArcFace distance from 0.416 to 0.282. Held-out NeRSemble results corroborate this advantage, and the qualitative comparisons show better preservation of facial structure, glasses, and hair.

Combining intermediate DINOv2 and SAM2.1 features provides a useful empirical contribution to perceptual supervision. Table 2 compares the combined loss against each component and LPIPS+L1; the combined features improve identity preservation and DreamSim. Supplementary analyses of layers and token types provide additional insight into complementary supervision signals.

The system integrates established components coherently: FLAME-anchored Gaussians, cross-attention from 3D tokens to image features, and mixed real, synthetic, and in-the-wild training. The data ablation supports the importance of multi-view supervision and the additional benefit of in-the-wild images.

The segmentation- and CLIP-conditioned extension demonstrates useful image- and text-guided control without text-specific training. The supplementary examples establish a credible practical application beyond reconstruction, although rigorous disentanglement remains unproven.

The supplement reports architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, training costs, evaluation identities, and cropping procedures. Overall, the consistent reconstruction gains and useful supervision study favor weak acceptance despite limitations in evaluation scale and claim calibration.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation covers only 11 Ava-256 and five NeRSemble identities, as disclosed in supplementary Section F. Exact view-pair counts, angular ranges, sampling procedures, and uncertainty estimates are missing. This limits confidence in broad generalization claims, particularly for small differences such as novel-view LPIPS of 0.269 versus 0.274.

The evidence supports a perceptual tradeoff more strongly than a general superiority claim for the loss. Against LPIPS+L1, the proposed loss leaves PSNR unchanged, worsens LPIPS from 0.285 to 0.291, and improves DreamSim and ArcFace modestly. The claimed high-frequency advantage lacks a region-specific or human perceptual evaluation. Equation 7's multiplicative combination is also neither motivated nor compared with an additive combination, and the claimed drop-in applicability is tested only within this system.

Architectural originality is primarily incremental, building on transformer reconstruction, foundation-model features, and template-anchored Gaussians. There are no controlled ablations isolating the added trainable encoder branch or omission of decoder self-attention. Consequently, the substantial gains over external baselines cannot be attributed cleanly between architecture, supervision, and different training data.

Claims of complete 3D consistency and arbitrary-view reconstruction exceed the measurements. Evaluation concerns rendered images rather than geometric accuracy or explicit cross-view consistency, and the final image-space sharpening CNN has no consistency constraint. Rear-facing Cafca views are discarded, while quantitative extreme-view tests emphasize opposing face views. The acknowledged temporal flickering further qualifies the consistency claim.

Editing is evaluated qualitatively, with the external comparison limited to one NeRFFaceEditing demo subject. There are no quantitative tests of geometry preservation, prompt adherence, identity stability, or unintended changes. Figure 20 also illustrates incomplete prompt control: several outputs under female prompts retain masculine facial characteristics. These results demonstrate conditional generation more clearly than fully disentangled editing.

Reproduction remains underspecified despite the useful supplementary details: image resolution, batch size, dataset sampling ratios, Gaussian displacement constants, and the detailed sharpening architecture are not provided. The sharpening model's training data are described inconsistently, with supplementary Section C.5 mentioning VFHQ while the training section refers to excluding Cafca from the reconstruction data. Minor presentation issues include Table 5 labeling values around 15–16 as SSIM, apparently instead of PSNR.

strengths: The reconstruction results support a useful contribution, especially for large viewpoint changes. On Ava-256 extreme views, PercHead achieves 15.9 PSNR, 0.291 LPIPS, and 0.282 ArcFace distance, compared with PanoHead’s 14.2, 0.349, and 0.416. Held-out NeRSemble results show a similar advantage (Tables 1 and 3), and the visual comparisons support improved facial structure and hair reconstruction.

The perceptual-supervision approach has meaningful controlled evidence. Table 2 compares conventional losses, individual foundation-model losses, their combination, training-data choices, and sharpening. Combining DINOv2 and SAM improves identity preservation over either component alone. Figure 18 additionally shows better robustness than LPIPS+L1 on challenging inputs with sharpening disabled.

The architecture and training recipe form a practical reconstruction system: image-conditioned Gaussian decoding combines multi-view supervision with limited in-the-wild data. The editing extension demonstrates useful segmentation-guided and zero-shot text-conditioned generation, with additional examples in the supplement.

The supplement provides architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, training times, evaluation identities, processing details, and lightweight variants. Overall, the demonstrated reconstruction improvements favor acceptance despite reservations about claim scope and evaluation depth.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation covers only 11 Ava-256 identities and five held-out NeRSemble identities (Supplement F). View-pair counts, precise angular coverage, subject-selection rationale, and uncertainty across identities are not reported. The results are promising, but this limits confidence in broad claims about arbitrary viewpoints and extreme out-of-distribution robustness.

The claimed general superiority of the new loss is stronger than the evidence. In Table 2, LPIPS+L1 matches the proposed loss in PSNR and achieves better LPIPS (0.285 versus 0.291); the proposed loss improves DreamSim and ArcFace. This supports a perceptual tradeoff rather than uniform improvement. Its claimed utility as a drop-in replacement is tested only within this reconstruction architecture and its editing extension.

The methodological novelty is primarily the combination of established components. The manuscript acknowledges prior DINO-based perceptual losses and builds on LAM-style feature extraction. It does not isolate the additional trainable encoder’s contribution or explain experimentally why the multiplicative DINOv2/SAM objective in Equation 7 is preferable to an additive combination.

Disentangled 3D editing remains qualitatively supported. A segmentation map constrains projected semantic regions but does not uniquely specify 3D geometry, while CLIP can encode both geometry and appearance. Figures 5, 19, and 20 show useful conditioning, but do not establish independent control or identity preservation. The comparison with NeRFFaceEditing uses one demo subject, and there are no quantitative measures of edit locality, geometry preservation, or prompt adherence.

The claims of complete 3D consistency exceed what the evaluation establishes. Metrics measure rendered-image agreement, without direct geometry or cross-view correspondence assessment. The view-wise sharpening CNN also has no explicit consistency constraint. Excluding back-facing training views and acknowledging temporal flicker further narrow the supported claim to improved novel-view rendering within the tested settings.

Reproducibility and presentation have correctable gaps: input/output resolutions, batch size, dataset sampling ratios, exact loss-network checkpoints, and Gaussian displacement hyperparameters are insufficiently specified. Section 3.4 says images are input into 'CLIP and FFHQ,' apparently confusing the dataset with an encoder, and Supplement Table 5 labels values around 15–16 as SSIM. These issues are secondary to the scientific reservations above.

strengths: The paper makes a useful contribution to single-image head reconstruction under large viewpoint changes. Its combination of a Gaussian decoder, mixed single-view/multi-view training, and foundation-model supervision is supported by quantitative improvements and convincing visual comparisons. Overall, the reconstruction evidence favors acceptance despite reservations about evaluation scale and broader claims.

Performance gains are strongest in the challenging extreme-view setting. On Ava-256, PercHead achieves 15.9 PSNR, 0.291 LPIPS, and 0.282 ArcFace distance, compared with PanoHead's 14.2, 0.349, and 0.416. Held-out NeRSemble results provide corroborating evidence: extreme-view LPIPS improves from the best baseline's 0.310 to 0.221. The improvements therefore extend beyond the proposed training features.

The ablations meaningfully separate training data, perceptual supervision, and sharpening. Table 2 shows that the combined DINOv2/SAM loss improves ArcFace distance over LPIPS+L1 from 0.300 to 0.282 and DreamSim from 0.115 to 0.106. Figure 8 supports improved hair detail, while supplementary experiments examine individual layers, token choices, and difficult inputs.

The editing extension demonstrates useful segmentation-guided control and image- or text-conditioned appearance without text-specific training. Supplementary architecture dimensions, optimizer settings, training times, evaluation identities, and lightweight variants also improve the manuscript's practical value and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is substantially smaller than the dataset names suggest: Supplement F lists only 11 Ava-256 identities and five held-out NeRSemble identities. Selection criteria, precise view-pair counts, and uncertainty estimates are not reported. This limits confidence in broad robustness claims, particularly for the smaller novel-view gains, although it does not negate the substantial extreme-view improvements.

The central loss contribution is narrower than the claims of a generally applicable drop-in replacement. Foundation-feature perceptual supervision has precedents acknowledged in Related Work, and the proposed combination is tested only within this pipeline. Table 2 shows unchanged PSNR and slightly worse LPIPS than LPIPS+L1, so the evidence supports a useful perceptual/identity tradeoff rather than uniformly superior supervision. There is also no comparison of the multiplicative combination in Eq. 7 against an additive combination.

Claims of complete 3D consistency and accurate unseen-region recovery exceed the measurements. Evaluation primarily measures rendered-image similarity; it does not directly assess geometry accuracy or consistency of the final images after the view-specific sharpening CNN. Back-of-head training views are explicitly discarded, further limiting evidence for arbitrary-view, complete-head reconstruction.

Disentangled editing is supported mainly by qualitative examples. A 2D segmentation map does not uniquely determine 3D geometry, and conditioning separately on segmentation and CLIP features does not establish disentanglement. The paper lacks quantitative measurements of geometry preservation, style leakage, and edit locality; comparison with NeRFFaceEditing is limited to its demo subject. The acknowledged loss of input identity also constrains personalized editing applications.

Some implementation details remain insufficient for faithful reproduction, including feature-loss preprocessing, dataset sampling proportions, Gaussian displacement bounds, and the sharpening network specification. Correctable presentation issues include the unexplained 'CLIP and FFHQ' statement in Section 3.4 and Table 5's apparent SSIM header over PSNR-scale values. These are secondary concerns rather than the main limitations determining the recommendation.
